Empirical Research Plan: “The Causal Effect of Boston and NYC Exam-School Attendance on Student Achievement”

------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------
Chosen method: Fuzzy Regression Discontinuity Design (FRD) combined with a local IV.

Justification
• Admission is determined by a known, sharp score cutoff that differs by school–cohort.  
• Students just above vs. just below the cutoff are plausibly comparable (quasi-random).  
• Because not every student offered a seat actually enrolls, assignment (offer) is the instrument and actual attendance is the endogenous treatment ⇒ FRD / local IV delivers the LATE of attending an elite exam school for applicants at the margin.

Optional extensions  
– Pool multiple cutoffs by re-centering the running variable (“score minus cutoff”) and add cutoff-fixed effects (Lee & Card, 2008).  
– Estimate separate effects for Boston vs. NYC or by gender/race.

------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
T_i = 1 if student i actually enrolls in an elite exam school in the fall following the exam; 0 otherwise.

Instrument  
Z_i = 1 if exam score ≥ school-year-specific cutoff (i.e., received an offer).  
Running variable R_i = ExamScore_i − Cutoff_sy.  
Cutoff at R_i = 0.

Control group  
Applicants with R_i just below 0 who therefore did not receive an offer.

Treatment timing / outcome reference  
• Event date: first day of 9th grade (Boston) or 10th grade (NYC) when placements materialize.  
• Outcomes measured 1–4 years later: state math & ELA tests, SAT, Regents, graduation, etc.

------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff (no other determinants jump).  
Plausible because (i) exams are centrally proctored, (ii) cutoffs are announced only after testing, (iii) families cannot precisely target the score.

A2. No precise manipulation of the running variable.  
Plausible; we will run McCrary density tests.

A3. Monotonicity / first-stage relevance (offer weakly increases probability of attendance, no “defiers”).  
Reasonable: it is hard to imagine someone who would attend only if NOT offered.

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no interference within the narrow local sample).  
Reasonable because treatment is school-level and the bandwidth is small relative to total enrollment.

A5. Homogeneous local bandwidth (covariate balance).  
We will document balance on pre-treatment covariates.

------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
------------------------------------------------
T1. Score manipulation (prep courses, re-takes).  
• Density test and covariate continuity tests.  
• Sensitivity checks dropping re-takers or using first-sitting scores.

T2. Differential attrition or outcome data coverage.  
• Verify symmetric attrition around cutoff.  
• Use administrative linkage to capture moves; include IPW re-weighting if necessary.

T3. Heterogeneous cutoffs across schools/cohorts creating compositional bias.  
• Re-center within each cutoff, include cutoff-FE.  
• Cluster standard errors by cutoff or by school-cohort.  
• Estimate city-specific effects.

------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast IV / RD regression
library(rdrobust)    # bias-corrected RD
library(rddensity)   # McCrary test

# 1. Load and stack cohorts
bos  <- read_csv("boston_exam_applicants.csv")
nyc  <- read_csv("nyc_exam_applicants.csv")

dat <- bind_rows(bos, nyc) %>%
  mutate(score_diff = exam_score - cutoff,          # running variable
         offer      = if_else(score_diff >= 0, 1, 0),
         attend     = if_else(enrolled_exam == 1, 1, 0),
         city       = factor(city),
         cutoff_id  = interaction(city, school, year) )

# 2. Select bandwidth (e.g., ±15 points) – can be data driven
bw <- 15
sample <- dat %>% filter(abs(score_diff) <= bw)

# 3. Main FRD: 2SLS local linear with cutoff-FE
main_iv <- feols( outcome_std ~ 1 | attend ~ offer, 
                  data = sample,
                  subset = abs(score_diff) <= bw,
                  cluster = ~cutoff_id,
                  nthreads = 4, 
                  vcov = "HC3",
                  weights = ~kernel_triangular(score_diff/bw) )

summary(main_iv)

# 4. McCrary density test
mcc <- rddensity(sample$score_diff)
summary(mcc)

# 5. Bias-corrected RD as robustness (intent-to-treat)
itt_rd <- rdrobust(y = sample$outcome_std, x = sample$score_diff, fuzzy = sample$attend)
summary(itt_rd)

# 6. Covariate balance check
covars <- c("gender", "race_black", "ell", "pre8_math")
bal <- map_dfr(covars, 
       ~ broom::tidy(feols(reformulate("offer", response = .x),
                           data = sample)))
print(bal)
```

------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------
Theory is ambiguous: peer quality ↑ but curriculum harder and cream-skimming lower. Prior studies suggest near-zero or modest positive impacts.

Prior guess: +0.05σ (5 percent of a standard deviation) on state math/ELA after 2 years. Effects on SAT and college enrollment likely similarly small positive (+0.03–0.07σ).

------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (FRD)
------------------------------------------------
C1: No manipulation of running variable …… 1  
C2: Covariates smooth at cutoff ………………… 1  
C3: Correct functional form / bandwidth …… 1  
C4: Strong first stage (F-stat > 10) ………… 1  
C5: No other policy change at cutoff ………… 1  

Total = 5/5 (all appear reasonably satisfied given the context, contingent on empirical tests).

------------------------------------------------
End of plan
